asked: We plan to import a skin-lightening cream containing mercury that is marketed for freckles and age spots. How does FDA treat it?
answer:
FDA does not permit the import or sale of a skin-lightening cream containing mercury marketed for freckles and age spots, as such preparations are misbranded and/or adulterated under 21 CFR 700.13. The use of mercury in cosmetic preparations intended for skin bleaching—such as removal or prevention of freckles and age spots—is prohibited except under specific conditions outlined in paragraph (d)(2) of section 700.13, which allows trace amounts of mercury only if they are unavoidable under good manufacturing practices and less than 1 part per million, or if the product is intended for use in the eye area with no effective nonmercurial substitute available. For a cream marketed for freckles and age spots (non-eye), these exceptions do not apply, so such a product would be misbranded and adulterated [5]. Any such preparation shipped after January 5, 1973 is subject to regulatory action [5].

21 CFR 700.13(a) states that mercury-containing cosmetic preparations intended for use as skin-bleaching agents or to remove freckles and/or brown spots are regarded as drugs as well as cosmetics [1].  
21 CFR 700.13(b) confirms the known toxicity of mercury compounds, including absorption through intact skin and accumulation in the body, leading to severe adverse effects such as allergic reactions and chronic irritation [2].  
21 CFR 700.13(c) notes that the effectiveness of mercury-containing preparations for skin bleaching is questionable and no well-controlled studies have been provided by the FDA to support this claim [3].  
21 CFR 700.13(d)(1) declares that any product containing mercury as a skin-bleaching agent offered for sale as such is misbranded under sections 502(a), (f)(1), and (f)(2), and may constitute an unapproved new drug in violation of section 505 [5].  
21 CFR 700.13(d)(2) states that any cosmetic containing mercury is regarded as adulterated unless it meets either condition: (i) contains no more than a trace amount of mercury less than 1 part per million, unavoidable under good manufacturing practice, or (ii) is intended for eye use only and contains no more than 65 parts per million of mercury with no effective nonmercurial preservative substitute available [6].  
21 CFR 700.13(d)(2)(i) specifies that the trace amount of mercury must be less than 1 part per million (0.0001 percent), calculated as metal, and unavoidable under good manufacturing practice [7].  
21 CFR 700.13(d)(2)(ii) permits use in eye-area cosmetics with no effective nonmercurial substitute if the mercury content does not exceed 65 parts per million (0.0065 percent), calculated as metal [8].

asked: Our aerosol hair spray uses vinyl chloride as a co-propellant at 2%. Is that permitted?
answer:
The use of vinyl chloride as a co-propellant at 2% in an aerosol hair spray is not permitted. Section 700.14(a) states that any cosmetic aerosol product containing vinyl chloride as an ingredient is deemed to be adulterated under section 601(a) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, and section 700.14(b) specifies that any such product shipped within the jurisdiction is subject to regulatory action. These provisions do not permit the use of vinyl chloride in cosmetic aerosol products, including hair sprays, regardless of concentration or form [1].

21 CFR 700.14(a) prohibits the use of vinyl chloride as an ingredient in cosmetic aerosol products, including hair sprays, because it is considered a deleterious substance that may render such products injurious to users [1].  
21 CFR 700.14(b) requires regulatory action for any cosmetic aerosol product containing vinyl chloride as an ingredient that is shipped within the jurisdiction of the Act [2].

asked: Our antimicrobial deodorant bar formula includes tribromsalan (TBS) at 0.25%. Can we sell it?
answer:
No, the antimicrobial deodorant bar containing tribromsalan (TBS) at 0.25% cannot be sold because tribromsalan is classified as a halogenated salicylanilide that renders any cosmetic product containing it injurious to users and thus adulterated under section 601(a) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act [2].  

The use of tribromsalan (TBS), dibromsalan (DBS), metabromsalan (MBS), or 3,3′,4,5′-tetrachlorosalicylanilide (TCSA) as an ingredient in any cosmetic product is prohibited because these substances are deemed deleterious and render the product injurious to users [2].  

Any cosmetic product containing these halogenated salicylanilides at any level for any purpose is considered adulterated under section 601(a) of the FD&C Act [2].  

The use of tribromsalan (TBS), including at a concentration of 0.25%, in a deodorant bar is not permitted because it is classified as a halogenated salicylanilide that causes photosensitization and can lead to severe, persistent skin disorders [1].  

These provisions impose no specific labeling, certification, or usage conditions for the ingredient; however, they establish that any product containing tribromsalan at any level is adulterated and therefore not allowed in interstate commerce after December 1, 1975 [3].

asked: We use chloroform as an extraction solvent for a botanical extract, and traces remain in our cream. Is the cream adulterated under the chloroform rule?
answer:
The cream is adulterated under the chloroform rule if traces of chloroform remain from its use as an extraction solvent, because any cosmetic product containing chloroform in residual amounts from processing as a solvent is considered adulterated and subject to regulatory action under sections 301 and 601(a) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act [2].

21 CFR 700.18(b) states that any cosmetic product containing chloroform in residual amounts from its use as a processing solvent during manufacture is adulterated and subject to regulatory action [2].

raw:
Yes, an exemption from the tamper-resistant rule for a vaginal product whose container cannot accept a seal is possible under specific conditions. A manufacturer or packer may request such an exemption by submitting a citizen petition under §10.30 of this chapter, clearly identified as a “Request for Exemption from Tamper-resistant Rule,” and including the required information to justify the exemption [4]. The exemption is not automatic but must be granted after review, and it is only available if the product's compliance with tamper-resistant packaging or labeling requirements is unnecessary or cannot be achieved [6]. The request must include a description of alternative steps taken or available to reduce the risk of malicious adulteration [7], and other information justifying the exemption may also be submitted [8].

The name of the product must be specified in the petition [5].

A manufacturer or packer may request an exemption from the packaging and labeling requirements, including for vaginal products, by submitting a citizen petition under §10.30 that includes the reasons why compliance with the tamper-resistant packaging or labeling requirements is unnecessary or cannot be achieved [6]. 

The request must include a description of alternative steps taken or available to reduce the likelihood of malicious adulteration [7].

Other information justifying an exemption may also be included in the petition [8].

Exemptions are not effective retroactively; they apply only after the FDA has reviewed and approved the petition, and the effective date for compliance with the tamper-resistant packaging requirement is generally set as of February 6, 1984 for products held for sale on or after that date, unless an exemption is granted [14]. However, if a manufacturer obtains an exemption, the requirement does not apply to that product during the period of the exemption [10].

The tamper-resistant packaging requirement applies only to products accessible to the public while held for sale; therefore, if the container cannot accept a seal and no alternative tamper-resistant feature is feasible, the exemption may be justified under the condition that the product's compliance with the rule is impossible or unnecessary [6]. 

Exemptions are not available for all vaginal products—specifically, the requirement applies to vaginal tablets, which have a different effective date (May 5, 1983), and exceptions must still meet the criteria of being necessary or achievable under the conditions outlined in §700.25(d) [13]. 

The exemption request is subject to review by the FDA and may be denied if the product can reasonably achieve tamper resistance through an alternative means, such as a distinctive indicator or barrier to entry that is not feasible due to container design constraints [6]. 

An exemption from the tamper-resistant rule for vaginal products whose containers cannot accept seals is possible only if the manufacturer submits a citizen petition under §10.30 with the name of the product, reasons why compliance is unnecessary or impossible, a description of alternative protective measures, and other supporting information justifying the exemption [5][6][7][8]. The exemption is not automatic and must be granted after review, and it does not apply retroactively; its effectiveness depends on FDA approval and is limited to products that are accessible to the public while held for sale [14]. 

The requirement for a tamper-resistant package applies only if the product is accessible to the public during retail sale, and exceptions may be granted under §700.25(d) when compliance cannot be achieved due to container design limitations [6][8].

asked: Our tinted moisturizer contains a UV filter only to protect the formula's color, and the label says 'with sunscreen.' How do we keep it a cosmetic?
answer:
To keep a tinted moisturizer containing a UV filter solely to protect the formula's color—and labeled with "with sunscreen"—as a cosmetic, the product must use the term “sunscreen” in its labeling only if accompanied by qualifying information that describes the nontherapeutic, nonphysiologic benefit (e.g., protection of color), and this qualifying statement must appear prominently and conspicuously on the label. Without such qualification, the use of "sunscreen" in labeling would cause the product to be regulated as a drug [1].

21 CFR 700.35(a) states that if a cosmetic contains a sunscreen ingredient and uses the term “sunscreen” or similar sun protection terminology in its labeling, the term must be qualified by describing the cosmetic benefit provided by the sunscreen ingredient [1].  
21 CFR 700.35(b) requires that the qualifying information—such as "Contains a sunscreen—to protect product color"—must appear prominently and conspicuously at least once in the labeling when the term “sunscreen” or similar sun protection terminology is used [2].

asked: We're designing a 4 oz lotion bottle. What must our ingredient list look like in terms of order and type size?
answer:
The ingredient list for a 4 oz lotion bottle is not addressed in 21 CFR 701.11 regarding order or type size. This regulation governs the statement of identity on the principal display panel and does not specify requirements for ingredient listing, ordering, or formatting.

21 CFR 701.11(a) requires that the principal display panel bear a statement of the identity of the commodity [1].  
21 CFR 701.11(b)(1) permits the common or usual name of the cosmetic as the statement of identity [3].  
21 CFR 701.11(b)(2) permits an appropriately descriptive name or a fanciful name understood by the public to identify the cosmetic when the nature is obvious [4].  
21 CFR 701.11(b)(3) permits an appropriate illustration or vignette representing the intended cosmetic use as the statement of identity [5].  
21 CFR 701.11(c) requires that the statement of identity be presented in bold type, in a size reasonably related to the most prominent printed matter on the panel, and in lines generally parallel to the base of the package [6].

When swapping an emollient due to a supplier shortage, the ingredient declaration must list each ingredient in descending order of predominance, using the name specified in §701.30 for that ingredient if available; otherwise, use the name adopted in the CTFA Cosmetic Ingredient Dictionary (Second Edition, 1977), with specific exclusions and exceptions listed in §701.3(c)(2)(i)(a) and (c)(2)(i)(b); if neither is applicable, then the ingredient may be designated by a name generally recognized by consumers, provided it does not fall under a color additive as defined in §701.3(g)(2)(iv). The declaration must appear prominently on the label or an affixed tag, and if space is insufficient, the Commissioner may establish an acceptable alternate format through regulation [1]. 

21 CFR 701.3(a) requires that each ingredient be declared by name in descending order of predominance, except fragrance or flavor, which may be listed as such; no ingredient may be designated as fragrance or flavor unless it is within the common consumer understanding of those terms [1].  
21 CFR 701.3(b) mandates that the ingredient declaration appear with prominence and conspicuousness so that ordinary individuals can read and understand it under normal purchase conditions, using letters not less than 1/16 inch in height and without being obscured by design or vignettes; if space is insufficient on the package, a firmly affixed tag, tape, or card may be used, and the Commissioner may establish an alternate acceptable format through regulation [2].  
21 CFR 701.3(c) specifies that a cosmetic ingredient shall be identified in the declaration by one of the following: (1) the name specified in §701.30; (2) if not available, the name adopted in the CTFA Cosmetic Ingredient Dictionary, Second Edition, 1977, with specific exclusions and additions as listed [4–6]; (3) if neither is applicable, by a name generally recognized by consumers [16].  
21 CFR 701.3(c)(2)(i) lists that certain names such as Acid Black 58, Acid Blue 168, and others are not adopted for cosmetic labeling; however, specific names like Benzophenone-11, Carbomer 934, and Amphoteric (all 20 numeric designations), Quaternium (all 49 numeric designations) are adopted for cosmetic use under conditions that require revised monographs to describe chemical compositions more precisely and be published by July 18, 1980 [6–12].  
21 CFR 701.3(c)(2)(ii) provides that the United States Pharmacopeia (USP), 19th Edition, 1975, and its supplements may be used as a source for ingredient designation if not otherwise specified in CTFA or USP [13].  
21 CFR 701.3(c)(2)(iii) allows the National Formulary, 14th Edition, 1975, and its supplements to be used as a source for ingredient designation [14].  
21 CFR 701.3(c)(2)(iv) permits use of the Food Chemicals Codex, Second Edition, 1972, with first and second supplements (1974, 1975), which are incorporated by reference [15].  
21 CFR 701.3(c)(3) allows a name generally recognized by consumers to be used if no other designation is available [16].  
21 CFR 701.3(g)(2)(iv) excludes an ingredient from being designated as fragrance or flavor if it is a color additive, and such exclusions must be considered when determining the appropriate name for labeling [17].  

Note: The provisions do not require specific actions beyond those listed above; however, if the swapped emollient contains a substance that is a color additive, then it cannot be labeled as fragrance or flavor unless it meets the criteria in §701.3(g)(2)(iv), and such designation would be prohibited [17]. The requirement to use the CTFA Dictionary (1977) applies only if no name is specified in §701.30, and certain names are excluded from use as listed in 21 CFR 701.3(c)(2)(i)(a) [6].

raw:
Yes, the bulk drums must carry consumer labeling if the shipment is not exempt under 21 CFR 701.9(a)(1) or (a)(2). The exemption from consumer labeling applies only when either (1) the person who introduced the shipment into interstate commerce is the operator of the establishment where it will be processed, labeled, or repacked, or (2) there is a written agreement between that person and the operator specifying the processing, labeling, or repacking conditions to ensure the cosmetic will not be adulterated or misbranded. In this case, since the shipment is sent to an unaffiliated contract filler who labels and packs it, and the shipper is not the operator of the filling establishment, the exemption applies only if a written agreement exists that specifies labeling requirements and ensures no adulteration or misbranding. If such an agreement is in place and followed, then the shipment may be exempt from consumer labeling during movement and holding; however, if the agreement is not provided or is refused for inspection, the exemption becomes void ab initio [3]. The exemption does not apply automatically and depends on the existence of a written agreement signed by both parties containing post office addresses and specifying processing, labeling, or repacking conditions to prevent adulteration or misbranding [3].

The requirement that the person who introduced the shipment into interstate commerce must have a written agreement with the operator of the establishment where it is labeled and packed, which includes specifications for labeling to ensure no adulteration or misbranding, is required by 21 CFR 701.9(a)(2) [3].  
The requirement that such person and the operator shall each keep a copy of the agreement until two years after the final shipment or delivery from the establishment is required by 21 CFR 701.9(a)(2) [3].  
The requirement that both parties must make copies of the agreement available for inspection at any reasonable hour to an FDA officer or employee who requests them is required by 21 CFR 701.9(a)(2) [3].  
The exemption from consumer labeling under paragraph (a)(2) becomes void ab initio if the operator refuses to make a copy of the agreement available for inspection, as specified in 21 CFR 701.9(c) [5].  
The exemption expires upon refusal by the operator to make a copy of the agreement available for inspection, as required under 21 CFR 701.9(d)(2) [8].  

These provisions do not require consumer labeling on the bulk drums if an exempting written agreement exists and is properly maintained and made available; however, without such an agreement or with refusal to provide it, the exemption does not apply and consumer labeling is required. The availability of a written agreement specifying labeling conditions to prevent misbranding is essential for any exemption [3].

raw:
Yes, you can leave the street address off the label and show only city, state, and ZIP code, provided that the street address is omitted because it appears in a current city or telephone directory [4]. The requirement to include the ZIP Code applies only to consumer commodity labels developed or revised after the effective date of this section; for nonconsumer packages, the ZIP Code must appear either on the label or in the labeling (including the invoice) [4].

The street address may be omitted if it is shown in a current city directory or telephone directory [4].  
The statement of the place of business shall include the street address, city, State, and ZIP Code; however, the street address may be omitted if it is shown in a current city directory or telephone directory [4].  
The requirement for inclusion of the ZIP Code shall apply only to consumer commodity labels developed or revised after the effective date of this section. In the case of nonconsumer packages, the ZIP Code shall appear either on the label or the labeling (including the invoice) [4].

This provision does not permit omitting city, state, and ZIP code entirely; the label must still include at least the city, state, and ZIP Code, with the street address being optional under the condition that it appears in a current directory [4].  
The requirement to show the place of business includes the city, state, and ZIP Code, and the omission of the street address is allowed only if it is available in a current city or telephone directory [4].

If the cosmetic is manufactured at a place other than the principal place of business, the label may state the principal place of business instead of the actual location, unless such statement would be misleading [5]. This exception does not apply to the omission of street address but could affect whether the principal place of business is appropriate for labeling purposes.  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to answer whether a non-consumer package must include city, state, and ZIP code if the street address is omitted—only that the ZIP Code must appear on the label or in labeling (including invoice) for consumer packages developed after the effective date [4]. For nonconsumer packages, the ZIP Code requirement applies only when it appears on the label or in labeling; however, no specific rule governs whether city and state are required if street address is omitted.

asked: We sell lipstick in a decorative compact-style case and a 0.15 oz lip balm. Where must the net quantity declaration go, and do the small containers give us any alternatives?
answer:
The net quantity declaration for lipstick in a decorative compact-style case must appear on the principal display panel; if the container is a "boudoir-type" container with capacity of one-fourth ounce or less, the principal display panel may be considered to be a tear-away tag affixed to the container, and the type size of the net quantity statement shall be governed by the dimensions of the decorative container [5]. For the 0.15 oz lip balm, which is a solid or semisolid cosmetic, the declaration must state the net quantity of contents that will be expelled when the instructions for use as shown on the container are followed and must appear on the principal display panel [9]. Small containers do not provide an alternative location for the net quantity declaration; instead, if the container is a boudoir-type with capacity one-fourth ounce or less, the principal display panel may be considered a tear-away tag affixed to the container, but the declaration still must appear on the principal display panel and shall be governed by the dimensions of the decorative container [5]. The net quantity must be expressed in terms of weight because the cosmetic is solid or semisolid [1]. The declaration shall accurately reveal the quantity of cosmetic in the package exclusive of wrappers and other material packed therewith [8]. The net quantity statement shall not include any term that tends to exaggerate the amount of cosmetic (e.g., “giant pint” or “full quart”) [7]. For a decorative compact-style case with capacity one-fourth ounce or less, the principal display panel may be considered a tear-away tag affixed to the container, and the type size shall be governed by the dimensions of the container [5]. The declaration must appear on the principal display panel within the bottom 30 percent of the label area, separated from other printed information by at least a space equal to the height of the lettering used in the quantity statement vertically and by at least twice the width of the letter “N” horizontally [7].

asked: Our 8 fl oz shampoo bottle has a 12-square-inch principal display panel. How must we declare net contents, and in what type size and position?
answer:
The net contents must be declared in square inches because the product is a liquid cosmetic and the principal display panel has an area of 12 square inches, which exceeds 5 but does not exceed 25 square inches. The declaration shall be expressed in terms of square inches, and if applicable (i.e., when the area is 1 square foot or more), the largest whole square unit(s) (such as square yards, square feet) shall follow in parentheses after the square inch value, with any remainder in square inches or common or decimal fractions of a square foot or yard. This requirement is based on 21 CFR 701.13(p).  

The type size of the net quantity of contents statement shall not be less than one-eighth inch in height because the principal display panel has an area of more than 5 but not more than 25 square inches. [10]  

The declaration must appear on the principal display panel and shall be placed within the bottom 30 percent of the area of the label panel, in line generally parallel to the base on which the package rests as it is designed to be displayed; however, this requirement does not apply when the declaration meets other requirements for packages with a principal display panel of 5 square inches or less. Since the principal display panel is 12 square inches (more than 5), the placement within the bottom 30 percent applies, as no exception is specified in the regulation. [6]  

The net quantity of contents shall be expressed in terms of square inches, and if applicable (i.e., when the area exceeds one square foot), the largest whole unit(s) shall follow in parentheses after the square inch value. [13]  

The declaration must appear as a distinct item on the principal display panel, separated from other printed label information by at least a space equal to the height of the lettering used in the declaration (above or below), and by at least a space equal to twice the width of the letter “N” of the style of type used in the quantity statement (to the left or right). raw:
The net contents must be declared in square inches because the product is a liquid cosmetic packaged in a bottle with a principal display panel of 12 square inches, which exceeds 5 but does not exceed 25 square inches. According to 21 CFR 701.13(p), when a package is labeled in terms of area measure, the declaration shall be expressed in terms of square inches and, if applicable (1 square foot or more), the largest whole square unit (square yards, square yards and square feet, square feet). The declaration in terms of the largest whole units shall be in parentheses following the declaration in terms of square inches and any remainder shall be in terms of square inches or common or decimal fractions of the square foot or square yard. For this 8 fl oz shampoo bottle with a 12-square-inch principal display panel, the net contents must be declared as square inches, and if applicable (i.e., if the area exceeds one square foot), the largest whole unit(s) should follow in parentheses. This requirement is based on 21 CFR 701.13(p).  

The type size of the net quantity of contents statement shall not be less than one-eighth inch in height because the principal display panel has an area of more than 5 but not more than 25 square inches, as specified in 21 CFR 701.13(i)(2).  

The declaration must appear on the principal display panel and shall be placed within the bottom 30 percent of the area of the label panel, in line generally parallel to the base on which the package rests as it is designed to be displayed; however, this requirement does not apply when the declaration meets other requirements for packages with a principal display panel of 5 square inches or less. Since the principal display panel is 12 square inches (more than 5), the placement within the bottom 30 percent applies, unless an exception exists—however, no such exception is specified in this case; therefore, it must be placed in the bottom 30 percent of the label panel [6].  

The requirement for placement within the bottom 30 percent does not apply when the declaration meets other requirements (e.g., size and type), but since the package has a principal display panel larger than 5 square inches, this exception does not trigger. Thus, the statement must be placed in the bottom 30 percent of the label panel [6].  

The net contents declaration shall appear as a distinct item on the principal display panel, separated from other printed label information by at least a space equal to the height of the lettering used in the declaration (above or below), and by at least a space equal to twice the width of the letter “N” of the style of type used in the quantity statement (to the left or right) [5].  

The net contents must be declared in square inches, with a minimum height of one-eighth inch for packages with a principal display panel between 5 and 25 square inches [10]. The declaration shall not include any term qualifying a unit that tends to exaggerate the amount (e.g., “giant pint”) [5].  

The net quantity of contents must be declared on the principal display panel, and if there is an alternate principal display panel, it shall be duplicated on each such panel [2].  

These provisions impose none regarding the specific font style or typeface; only the minimum height based on panel size is specified. The exact font or styling is not required beyond the minimum height requirement.  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to answer whether a numerical count, linear measure, or weight can be used instead of square inches for this liquid cosmetic—only that if there is a firmly established general consumer usage and trade custom, such terms may be used [1]. However, since the product is liquid and the container has a principal display panel larger than 5 square inches, and no such custom is specified in the sources, the requirement to use fluid measure applies only if such a custom exists. In this case, since it does not, the declaration must follow the area-based rule [1].  

The net contents must be declared in terms of square inches, with a minimum height of one-eighth inch, and placed on the principal display panel within the bottom 30 percent of the label panel, unless the package has a principal display panel of 5 square inches or less—this does not apply here [10][6]. The declaration must be in letters and numerals with uniform size for packages of substantially the same size [7].  

The net quantity of contents shall be expressed in terms of square inches, and if applicable (i.e., when the area is 1 sq. ft. or more), the largest whole square unit(s) shall follow in parentheses after the square inch value, with any remainder in square inches or decimal fractions of a square foot or yard [13].  

The net quantity statement must not include qualifying terms that exaggerate the amount (e.g., “giant pint”) [5].  

The declaration must be on the principal display panel and duplicated if there are alternate principal display panels [2].  

The requirement for placement within the bottom 30 percent of the label panel applies, as the principal display panel is 12 square inches—more than 5 but less than 25—so it falls under the condition in 21 CFR 701.13(f)(1) that does not apply to packages with ≤5 sq. in. [6].  

The net contents must be declared in terms of square inches, and if applicable (i.e., when the area exceeds one square foot), the largest whole unit(s) shall follow in parentheses after the square inch value [13].
